issues.legal_issue: A revisional authority may treat an occupant’s prolonged use of premises to operate a licensed business and the resulting hardship as relevant to whether eviction is inexpedient, and an order based on those considerations is not liable to be quashed for an apparent error of law.
material_facts: The occupant had used the premises to conduct a cinema for many years and did so under a licence granted by the District Magistrate.
The State Government considered the occupant’s continued possession and cinema business when deciding that eviction was inexpedient.
The District Magistrate had earlier released the premises to the owners on the ground that they required it for their own occupation.
issues.conclusion: The State Government’s decision was based on relevant considerations and disclosed no apparent error of law; the High Court was not justified in quashing it, and the challenge to that decision failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7-A(1), including its proviso, gives the District Magistrate discretion not to order eviction where there has been undue delay or eviction is otherwise inexpedient. The wide language of the proviso leaves the authority to consider relevant circumstances. The State Government may exercise that discretion in revision under Section 7-F, and a decision based on relevant considerations is not liable to be set aside for an apparent error of law.

rule.if: challenge_to_revisional_eviction_decision and occupant_used_premises_for_years and occupant_operated_licensed_business and authority_considered_hardship

predicates.challenge_to_revisional_eviction_decisio: A party challenged in court a revisional authority’s decision refusing to order an occupant’s eviction.
predicates.occupant_used_premises_for_years: The occupant had remained in possession and used the premises over a prolonged period.
predicates.occupant_operated_licensed_business: The occupant conducted a business in the premises under a licence granted by a public authority.
predicates.authority_considered_hardship: The authority considered the hardship to the occupant arising from eviction.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a revisional eviction decision and the authority considered an occupant’s prolonged use, licensed business, and resulting hardship, the decision remains undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A prior release decision based on the owner’s bona fide need does not prevent the authority from later considering whether eviction of the occupant is inexpedient.
material_facts: The premises had been released to the owners on the ground that they bona fide required it for their own occupation.
The later eviction proceeding gave the occupant an opportunity to raise circumstances making eviction inexpedient.
The State Government considered the occupant’s circumstances when deciding the revision against the eviction order.
issues.conclusion: The earlier release decision did not preclude the authority from exercising its discretion against eviction in the later proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The release inquiry concerned whether the owners bona fide required the premises. The circumstances relevant to whether eviction was inexpedient under the proviso to Section 7-A could be raised by the occupant at the later eviction stage, so the earlier decision did not foreclose that inquiry.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_followed_release_dec: An eviction proceeding took place after an authority had released the premises to the owner.
predicates.release_decision_addressed_owner_need: The earlier release decision addressed whether the owner bona fide required the premises for personal occupation.
predicates.occupant_could_raise_later_evicting_circ: The occupant had an opportunity in the later eviction proceeding to present circumstances against eviction.

issues.definition: When a release decision addressed the owner’s need and the occupant could present eviction-related circumstances in a later proceeding, the earlier decision does not bar later consideration of those circumstances.

issues.legal_issue: A person who becomes a tenant under a lease between the parties remains a tenant protected against an eviction suit requiring prior administrative permission, even if the lease was made without an allotment order.
material_facts: The landlord leased the premises to the occupant, who paid rent under the lease.
No allotment order had been made for the occupant.
The owners brought a civil suit to recover possession without first obtaining the District Magistrate’s permission.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was a tenant for purposes of the statutory protection, and the suit was not maintainable because it had been brought without the required permission.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(g) and 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 define a tenant by reference to rent payable and restrict eviction suits without prior permission. Under Udho Dass v. Prem Prakash (1963 A.L.J. 406), a lease made without an allotment order may create a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties even though it does not bind the authorities. Reading the definition and scheme of the Act, a tenant without an allotment order is still protected by Section 3; the landlord is estopped from denying that status.

rule.if: eviction_civil_suit and lease_created_tenancy_between_parties and occupant_paid_rent_under_lease and no_prior_permission_obtained and no_allotment_order_made

predicates.eviction_civil_suit: A landlord brought a civil suit seeking to evict an occupant.
predicates.lease_created_tenancy_between_parties: The landlord and occupant entered a lease that created a tenancy between them.
predicates.occupant_paid_rent_under_lease: The occupant paid rent under the lease.
predicates.no_prior_permission_obtained: The landlord brought the suit without first obtaining the required permission from the responsible authority.
predicates.no_allotment_order_made: No administrative allotment order had been made in favour of the occupant.

issues.definition: When an occupant is a rent-paying tenant under a lease, an eviction suit is not maintainable if it was brought without prior permission, even though no allotment order was made.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot waive by agreement the statutory protection against an eviction suit brought without prior permission when that protection is founded on public policy.
material_facts: The lease stated that neither party would claim the benefit of the rent-control legislation and that its provisions would not apply to the lease.
The owners brought an eviction suit without first obtaining the District Magistrate’s permission.
The statutory protection was intended to protect tenants as a weaker class and to require an authority to consider the landlord’s claim and the tenant’s needs.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not barred by the lease from relying on the statutory protection; the agreement could not waive that protection, and the suit was not maintainable without permission.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 is prohibitive and protects tenants from eviction suits without permission. Although a person may waive a statutory benefit enacted solely for private benefit when no public policy is involved, this protection rests on public policy because it protects a weaker class and serves the community interest. Under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement whose object defeats a provision of law is void. Lachoo Mal v. Radhey Shyam recognizes waiver only where public policy does not prevent it; the Court also refers to Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya in discussing public policy.

rule.if: eviction_suit_under_tenant_protection_regime and agreement_disclaims_tenant_protection and suit_filed_without_required_permission and protection_serves_public_policy

predicates.eviction_suit_under_tenant_protection_re: A landlord brought a suit to evict a tenant in a regime that restricts eviction suits.
predicates.agreement_disclaims_tenant_protection: The landlord and tenant agreed that the tenant would not claim the statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.suit_filed_without_required_permission: The landlord filed the suit without first obtaining the required administrative permission.
predicates.protection_serves_public_policy: The protection is intended to safeguard a weaker class and serves a public interest beyond the parties’ private interests.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit is brought without required permission and the parties’ agreement disclaims protection that serves public policy, the tenant cannot waive that protection.
